reviews.scope: verifying element membership in the target set
reviews.reason: Certifying that a set has infinitely many members requires understanding what a set is and verifying that every constructed object satisfies the defining membership conditions as an element.

reviews.scope: constructing reciprocal-integer rational families to certify infinitude
reviews.reason: Building an indexed family of unit fractions 1/n relies on rational number classification, whereas certifying infinitude for unbounded integer sets or geometric midpoint sequences does not use rational classifications.
reviews.counterexample: Proving the set of even positive integers is infinite using the indexed family 2n for positive integers n avoids fractions and rational number classification.

reviews.scope: representing an indexed family of planar coordinate points
reviews.reason: Verifying that an indexed family of ordered pairs lies in a planar region requires Cartesian coordinates, but certifying infinitude of scalar number sets or synthetic geometric sets needs no coordinates.
reviews.counterexample: Certifying that the interval (0,1) contains infinitely many real numbers via the scalar sequence 1/(n+1) requires no planar coordinate system.

reviews.scope: basic principal and interest-rate vocabulary before multi-period discounting
reviews.reason: Single-period simple interest introduces principal and rate terminology that prepares for contrasting add-on charges with effective rates, although multi-period loan equations discount dated cash flows rather than computing simple interest.
reviews.counterexample: A student can write and solve the discounted cash-flow equation P = sum of c_k (1+r)^(-k) directly from periodic growth factors without computing one-year simple interest.

reviews.scope: summing equal discounted periodic installments in closed form
reviews.reason: When periodic loan repayments are equal, their discounted present values form a finite geometric progression summed by formula, whereas unequal repayments or two-period schedules are summed term by term.
reviews.counterexample: Modeling a two-installment loan or a loan with varying seasonal payments sums the individual discounted terms directly without the finite geometric series formula.

reviews.scope: approximating the periodic rate of a cash-flow equation by bisection
reviews.reason: Bracketed interval bisection is one numerical procedure to approximate the unique periodic rate of a monotone net-present-value equation, while two-period loans or Newton iteration determine the rate without bisection.
reviews.counterexample: For a two-period installment loan, the periodic discount factor satisfies a quadratic equation that can be solved algebraically in closed form without interval bisection.

reviews.scope: setting up the x-axis standard hyperbola equation for substitution
reviews.reason: Algebraic elimination commonly substitutes a line equation into the standard x-axis hyperbola equation x^2/a^2 - y^2/b^2 = 1, whereas geometric asymptote-slope arguments or rectangular hyperbolas xy = k avoid this form.
reviews.counterexample: Counting intersections of lines with the rectangular hyperbola xy = 1 or reasoning geometrically from branch tangents and asymptote directions avoids the standard equation x^2/a^2 - y^2/b^2 = 1.

reviews.scope: identifying one-point nontangent intersections via asymptote slopes
reviews.reason: Comparing a line's slope against the standard asymptote slopes +/-b/a geometrically identifies one-point nontangent intersections, while algebraic substitution detects the same case directly from a vanishing quadratic leading coefficient.
reviews.counterexample: Substituting y = kx + m into the hyperbola equation and checking when the x^2 coefficient vanishes counts one-point nontangent intersections algebraically without invoking separate asymptote equations.

reviews.scope: counting real intersections via the quadratic discriminant when degree is two
reviews.reason: In the algebraic elimination route, once the quadratic leading coefficient is confirmed nonzero, the discriminant counts zero, one, or two intersections, whereas geometric slope and tangent comparisons avoid computing discriminants.
reviews.counterexample: Comparing a line through the origin against the asymptote slopes +/-b/a determines whether it meets the hyperbola in zero or two points geometrically without evaluating a quadratic discriminant.

reviews.scope: combining intersection counts of two lines via union inclusion-exclusion
reviews.reason: Counting total hyperbola intersections with two intersecting lines uses the two-set union cardinality formula to subtract a shared intersection point, whereas single-line intersection problems do not involve set unions.
reviews.counterexample: Determining whether a single line meets a hyperbola in 0, 1, or 2 points requires no finite set-union or inclusion-exclusion counting.

reviews.scope: perpendicular line directions and right angles
reviews.reason: Defining a line to be perpendicular to a plane when its direction is orthogonal to every direction in that plane directly relies on the meaning of perpendicular lines and right angles.

reviews.scope: foundational concepts of lines and planes as geometric objects
reviews.reason: Stating the universal condition that a spatial line is perpendicular to every line in a plane presupposes the primitive geometric notions of lines and planar surfaces introduced in basic solid geometry.

reviews.scope: contrasting the universal definition with the two-intersecting-lines criterion
reviews.reason: The two-intersecting-lines determination theorem is a finite sufficient criterion contrasted with the all-directions definition, not a prior prerequisite needed to state or understand the definition of line-plane perpendicularity itself.
reviews.counterexample: One states and interprets the all-directions definition of line-plane perpendicularity prior to proving or applying the two-intersecting-lines determination theorem.

reviews.scope: meaning and positive domain of logarithms
reviews.reason: Understanding and applying the bound ln(t) <= t - 1 for t > 0 and its general-base scaling log_a(t) = ln(t)/ln(a) requires the definition of logarithms on positive real arguments.

reviews.scope: base-2 and base-10 change-of-base cases preparing for natural-log scaling
reviews.reason: Familiarity with converting logarithms to base 2 or 10 prepares students for rewriting log_a(t) as ln(t)/ln(a), though the prerequisite node is restricted to bases 2 and 10 rather than base e.
reviews.counterexample: Working strictly with the natural logarithm inequality ln(t) <= t - 1 or deriving log_a(t) = ln(t)/ln(a) directly from a^(log_a(t)) = t bypasses base-2 and base-10 conversion.

reviews.scope: proving the inequality via derivative sign and monotonicity
reviews.reason: Analyzing the sign of the derivative of ln(t) - t + 1 on (0,1) and (1,infinity) provides a standard calculus strategy for proving the bound, alongside integral or exponential-tangent arguments.
reviews.counterexample: Bounding ln(t) = integral from 1 to t of (1/u) du by comparing 1/u with 1 on (0,1) and (1,infinity) proves ln(t) <= t - 1 without derivative monotonicity.

reviews.scope: ordering data and identifying the middle value or middle pair
reviews.reason: Characterizing the points that minimize total distance to a finite dataset as the unique median for odd size or the closed interval between middle values for even size requires the median definition.

reviews.scope: comparing and adding line segment lengths in paired-endpoint proofs
reviews.reason: Comparing and summing segment lengths supports the geometric proof that placing a point between symmetric outer endpoints minimizes its combined distance to them, though an algebraic slope-counting argument avoids segment comparison.
reviews.counterexample: Analyzing the piecewise-linear derivative (number of points to the left minus number of points to the right) of sum |x - x_i| proves optimality algebraically without geometric segment comparison.

reviews.scope: expressing undirected number-line distances as absolute value differences
reviews.reason: Formulating the total distance objective algebraically as the sum of |x - x_i| relies on absolute value notation and its distance interpretation, whereas a geometric nested-interval pairing proof avoids absolute values.
reviews.counterexample: Pairing the outermost points on a line and observing geometrically that any point inside the segment [a,b] has distances summing to b - a proves the minimum without absolute value notation.

reviews.scope: rounding-based sum estimation as a concrete introductory example
reviews.reason: Rounding addends to tens or hundreds to estimate a sum provides a concrete elementary example that prepares for understanding the general purpose of numerical estimation across arbitrary operations and plausibility checks.
reviews.counterexample: A student can understand and apply numerical estimation using leading-digit multiplication or quotient magnitude checks without specifically rounding addends in an addition problem.

reviews.scope: concept of an angle between two rays sharing an endpoint
reviews.reason: Recognizing that the projected coordinate axes in an oblique dimetric drawing meet at 45 or 135 degrees while representing perpendicular spatial axes requires the basic geometric concept of an angle.

reviews.scope: distinguishing the projected axis angle convention from length foreshortening
reviews.reason: Preserving horizontal lengths while halving vertical lengths and setting the projected axes at 45 or 135 degrees are companion rules of oblique dimetric drawing; neither convention is derived from the other.
reviews.counterexample: Recognizing that the drawn coordinate axes meet at 45 or 135 degrees in an oblique dimetric diagram does not require applying the one-half vertical length scaling rule.
